criteria.descriptor: Correctly and precisely characterizes short-term memory as the in-context conversation buffer bounded by the context window and long-term memory as an externally persisted store recalled across sessions; describes real implementation mechanisms (summary/sliding-window buffers; database/vector store with explicit write and selective retrieval) without factual errors such as claiming a bigger context window equals long-term memory or that memory comes from fine-tuning.

Covers both memory types AND both complaints: defines each type, gives an implementation for each, correctly diagnoses complaint (1) as short-term/context and complaint (2) as long-term, and offers a concrete fix for each. Loses marks for skipping a definition, an implementation, a diagnosis, or a fix.

Justifies WHY each complaint maps to its memory type — e.g. that early turns fall out of scope because they exceed the context window, and that cross-session recall requires state persisted outside the window with selective retrieval — rather than merely asserting the mapping.

Clear, well-organized explanation using correct vocabulary (context window, conversation buffer, summarization/windowing, persistence, retrieval/embeddings); the short-term vs long-term distinction and the two mappings are easy to follow.

expected_answer_points: Short-term memory is the current session's working context — the running conversation/message history passed to the model each turn — held in the context window and therefore ephemeral and bounded by the token limit
Long-term memory is information persisted outside the context window (in a database, key-value store, or vector/embedding store) so it can be recalled across separate sessions
Long-term memory is used selectively: entries are written explicitly and only relevant items are retrieved (keyed lookup or semantic search) and injected into the prompt — not all loaded every turn
Complaint (1), forgetting early details in one long chat, is a short-term / context-window limitation caused by history exceeding the window
Fix for (1): manage the buffer — summarize/compress older turns, use a sliding window, or trim/retrieve so the relevant history fits the context window
Complaint (2), not recognizing a returning customer in a new session, is a long-term memory gap requiring persistence keyed to the customer
Fix for (2): persist customer identity, past tickets, and session summaries in an external store and retrieve/inject them at the start of a new session
common_pitfalls: Treats 'memory' as one undifferentiated thing, or claims a larger context window is itself long-term memory, missing that long-term memory must live outside the window and persist across sessions
Maps the complaints backwards — blaming the in-chat forgetting on missing long-term memory, or the returning-customer problem on the context window
Says long-term memory means loading everything the agent ever saw into the prompt every turn, ignoring selective retrieval and the fact that it would overflow the context window
Claims you give the agent memory by fine-tuning the model on the conversation, confusing model weights with runtime state/memory
Hand-waves 'just use a vector database' without explaining the explicit write step, keyed/semantic retrieval, or what short-term memory is
Assumes short-term/conversation memory automatically persists across sessions, so no separate long-term store is needed
reference_answer:
Short-term memory is the agent's working context for the current session: the running message history (conversation buffer) that is passed back into the model on every call. It lives inside the model's context window, so it is ephemeral and bounded by the token limit — nothing survives once the session ends, and old turns fall out of scope once the history grows past what fits.

Long-term memory is information deliberately persisted OUTSIDE the context window so it can be recalled across sessions. It's stored in an external store — a database, key-value store, or vector store of embeddings — written to explicitly (e.g. a per-customer summary or extracted facts saved after a session) and read back selectively via a keyed lookup or semantic retrieval, then injected into the prompt when relevant.

Complaint (1) — forgetting earlier details within one long chat — is a short-term / context-window failure: the early turns no longer fit. Fix it by managing the buffer: summarize or compress older turns (summary buffer), use a sliding window, or trim/retrieve the relevant history so it stays within the window.

Complaint (2) — not recognizing a returning customer next week — needs long-term memory: persist the customer's identity, past tickets, and a session summary keyed by customer id (or embedded for semantic search), and retrieve and inject the relevant entries at the start of the new session.
